newsitem.title: UK: Devaluation spectre still haunts Britain's Labour.
newsitem.headline: Devaluation spectre still haunts Britain's Labour.

text.p: As markets digest the idea that the next British election could end 17 years of Conservative government, Labour's would-be rulers remain haunted by memories of sterling's tribulations when it previously held power.

Almost 30 years after the government of prime minister Harold Wilson was forced to devalue sterling, and 20 years since the pound dived against the dollar, Labour is dogged by concern that its return to power could spell trouble for the currency.

It is those ghosts which Labour leader Tony Blair and shadow chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown have sought to lay to rest with their oft-stated commitment to a robust British currency, now valued at $1.5630.
"Clearly, we want a strong pound, and nobody would say otherwise," Brown told a news conference last year.
Labour has been at pains to assure the market that it will run a tight financial ship if it wins the next election, which must be held by May 1997.
But old fears die hard.

"It's part of the overall suspicion that Labour might still run a loose economic policy and that in turn would result in a depreciation of sterling," David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy, said on Friday.
"Labour are saying all the right things but there will always be that little element of doubt because of their history," he said.

In 1976, three years before Labour lost power to the Conservatives who have ruled ever since, sterling began at $2.02 but hit a low of $1.56 before ending the year down 17 percent on the dollar and 25 percent on the mark.

The chief explanation, experts say, lay in growing investor concerns over the future of the British economy. That was largely due to a languishing business sector and the government's failure to contain public spending enough to curb money supply growth.
This concern was typified by a headline the Wall Street Journal ran in April 1975 -- Good-Bye to Great Britain -- that advised investors to get out of British assets.

A deficit-swelling 1976 budget, public sector unrest, wage settlements in breach of a pay restraint policy, falling GDP and 17-1/2 percent annual money supply growth all took their toll on the value of sterling at various times throughout the year.
On September 8, 1976, the Bank of England stopped supporting the pound. By September 28, it stood at $1.63, having shed a hefty 6-1/2 cents in just two days.

Then Chancellor of the Exchequer Denis Healey, about to fly to Hong Kong for a Commonwealth finance ministers' meeting en route for the IMF annual meeting in Manila, turned back at the airport and soon afterwards announced that Britain was seeking a 2,300 million pound loan from the International Monetary Fund.
The year 1967 is another blot on Labour's economic copybook.

Then, too, worries about the economy and strikes hammered sterling. Rumours the government was seeking a huge IMF loan gripped the markets, culminating on November 17 in massive selling of pounds with only one buyer -- the Bank of England.
The next day the Treasury announced a 14.3 percent devaluation of sterling -- which was still pegged within the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system -- from $2.80 to $2.40.
"This does not mean that the pound in your pocket...has been devalued," declared prime minister Wilson in a phrase which was to dog him as the inevitable price rises began to be felt.
Many commentators believe, however, that Labour's horror of devaluation prevented it taking that much-needed step earlier.
"We can time, almost to the hour, the moment when the trajectory of Harold Wilson's career tilted from triumph to disaster," said leading political analyst Peter Kellner.

"In the early evening of Saturday, October 17, 1964, barely 24 hours after entering Downing Street, he decided to preserve the pound's value. That decision crippled his plans to revive Britain's economy," Kellner wrote in the Sunday Times.
A commentary in the Guardian newspaper after Wilson's death last year talked of the Labour Party's "almost endemic paranoia with the word "devaluation' as well as the substance".

Wilson's "devaluation phobia" could be traced back directly to his experience as President of the Board of Trade when the government was forced to devalue under humiliating circumstances in 1949 and lost the general election in 1951, the paper said.

That phobia was illustrated again this decade, just before the pound crashed out of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992. Labour could not bring itself to acknowledge that sterling was overvalued in the ERM lest it was again branded the party of devaluation, commentators say.
But Labour is by no means the only party to have suffered currency devaluations, analysts are quick to point out.
Sterling's 15 percent slide within six weeks of leaving the ERM was arguably the most embarrassing devaluation of all time -- and it occurred under a Conservative government.
